extracted.intended_audience: TeX users and authors typesetting mathematics (mathematicians, technical authors, TeX programmers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for producing well-formed mathematical typesetting with (plain) TeX: spacing, punctuation, delimiters, macros, boxes, displays, and other typography issues encountered when preparing math manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation placement in math
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation that belongs to a sentence should not be included in a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not put sentence punctuation inside math mode; end-of-sentence punctuation belongs to the surrounding text, not the formula. Example: punctuation that belongs to a sentence should not be included in a formula (16.8, 18.17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Always brace superscripts and subscripts when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not leave out any of the braces shown for superscripts/subscripts; superscripts and subscripts can be given in either order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use braces as in p_1'{e_1} and a_{b_{c_{d_e}}}; do not write $10,..10$ (which would be wrong). Both h' '_n and h_n' ' work, but omitting braces may produce errors (16.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \left and \right for scalable delimiters and to confine \over
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconfined \over applies to everything following it; use \left and \right (or similar) to make delimiters the correct size and to limit scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of an unconfined \over, use constructions like $$x= igl( rac{y+2}{k+1} igr)$$ or \left( ... \right) to make parentheses larger and to prevent \over from affecting unintended parts of the formula (17.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \mathcode changes sparingly and locally
rubrics_metrics.description: You can change the \mathcode of characters (e.g., make an ordinary period act like \cdot), but such changes should be confined to places where every instance should behave that way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: defining \mathcode'. to make periods act like \cdot is possible, but dangerous because ordinary periods are used frequently in displayed equations; confine the change to limited contexts (16.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with primes and subscripts together
rubrics_metrics.description: The interaction of primes and subscripts can produce unexpected positions/heights and sometimes does not work correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The second alternative (using a construction where a prime and a subscript occur simultaneously) may not behave properly; some mathematicians also use \prime inside subscripts which can complicate spacing and heights. Prefer explicit bracing or alternate constructions (16.4–16.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Script/superscript sizing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Different style levels (text, script, scriptscript) are used for superscripts and nested superscripts; choose correct styles so each level uses the appropriate font size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: style D is used for the subformula p', style S for the superscript e' and the subscript 2, and SS for supersuperscript prime; square root sign and base appear in text size while nested exponents appear in script and scriptscript (17.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Displayed multi-line formulas normally two lines tall
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas that are more than one line tall are usually two lines tall, not 1½ or 2½ lines tall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid displays whose height is an odd fraction of a line; aim for natural two-line tall constructions when a formula spans multiple lines (17.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bigger slashes/operations between big delimiters
rubrics_metrics.description: When a division slash sits between large parentheses, use a larger slash or special construction ( ig/,  igl/ igr) so the slash scales with delimiters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructs such as \bigl( ... \bigr) \big/ or specific macros to ensure a slash is appropriate in size between big parentheses (17.12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't include sentence-level commas/commas-in-math incorrectly
rubrics_metrics.description: Commas and punctuation are part of the sentence, not the formula; putting them inside math mode can lead to wrong spacing and prevent line breaks where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., writing commas in math mode can make TeX use smaller spaces and can change breakpoints; instead write the punctuation in the text outside the math formula (18.17, 18.22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-optimize keystrokes at expense of correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid trying to do everything with the fewest keystrokes; missing braces or shortcuts can lead to error messages and confusing code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: redundant braces can be safer than clever shortcuts; don't try to eliminate braces just to save keystrokes (18.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with \it and font changes inside math
rubrics_metrics.description: \it (text italic) and other text-font switches are not available in math script sizes and can cause errors if used throughout a formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If \it were used throughout a formula, subscripts in script font might be undefined; use proper math fonts or switch to text mode where appropriate (18.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \mathsurround and glue considerations for formula breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Line breaks do not occur at glue of any kind within math formulas; some constructions must be displayed rather than broken across lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complicated sets or predicates that would require line breaks, prefer displaying the formula rather than attempting to break it inside math mode (18.22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \sumprime or similar to control prime placement on sums
rubrics_metrics.description: To typeset a sum with a prime (like \sum'), special handling is needed so the prime and limits position nicely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define a \sumprime_#1 macro (example provided) that computes appropriate kerns and placements so the prime does not produce misaligned limits (18.44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious redefining delimiter codes (\delcode)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting \delcode to inappropriate values can mask errors and later cause strange failure modes for \left/\bigl etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If \delcode is set to a nonnegative delimiter code you might get no error for incorrect input (e.g., \left'), but strange effects will occur later. It's safer to keep standard delimiter codes and use explicit named macros for delimiters (17.21–17.22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide control sequence names for delimiters
rubrics_metrics.description: Because \left can balk if the next character is a left brace, it's best to have control sequence names for all delimiters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define named macros for delimiters and use \bigl/\biggr variants or custom macros to ensure consistent behavior; use \biggl/\biggr and variants when needed (17.22, 18.37).

rubrics_metrics.name: Change a character's math class when necessary (e.g., '*')
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters like '*' may be treated as binary operators in math mode, leading to unwanted extra spacing; adjust via grouping or change \mathcode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid extra medium spaces for patterns like (***) use constructions like \eqno ( *{*}*) ) or change the \mathcode of '*' if you never use it as a binary operator (19.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Switch math styles deliberately (\textstyle vs \displaystyle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide when a subformula should be in text style vs display style and use \textstyle or \displaystyle as needed; using \hbox around \displaystyle has different glue behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Switching to text style is common in multiline formulas; wrapping a display in an \hbox freezes glue at its natural width and invokes \everymath—be aware of these effects (19.2–19.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising equation numbers affects interline spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Raising an equation number increases the line height and can introduce unwanted extra space; use \smash or careful placement to avoid it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you raise an equation number, TeX increases the line height and puts extra space between that line and the previous one. Use \smash{\raise...} to avoid increasing the natural height (19.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate alignment macros and understand centering/spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Macros like \eqalign, \eqalignno, and \displaylines center boxes and determine where alignment tabs (&) and equation numbers appear; design displays with that behavior in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., an \eqalign box is centered and its internal & alignments are local, so the placement of conjunction words or numbers may be different than expected. Use \eqalignno when equation numbers on the right are desired and be mindful of \cr and \noalign spacing (19.9–19.14, 19.16–19.19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer copying boxes for repeated text for efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same paragraph or content must be repeated many times, build it once in a box and \copy it rather than retypesetting each time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set the repeated text into \setbox0=\vbox{...} and then use \copy0 repeatedly; it's much faster and saves processing time. Use \strut inside boxed paragraphs to preserve interbaseline distances (20.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ## in macro definitions when replacement text contains definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a macro whose replacement text itself contains parameter tokens (or \def inside), use ## to represent a parameter # in the inner definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \def\a#1{\def\b##1{##1#1}} results in \a! expanding to \def\b#1{#1!}. The ## feature is indispensable in such nested-definition cases (20.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Know semantics of \let vs macro definition
rubrics_metrics.description: \let copies the current meaning of a control sequence; \def (and \gdef) create macros that expand later using the then-current tokens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want variable \b to be fixed at its current meaning in \a, use \let; if you want \a to expand into the token \b (whose meaning is whatever it is at time of use), use \def. Use \let to interchange meanings of control sequences (20.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter passing and bracing between macros
rubrics_metrics.description: When passing parameters from one macro to another, parameters have to percolate down and should be enclosed in braces to preserve them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define \mustnt#1#2{I must not #1 in #2.\par} and higher-level macros that call it should pass arguments with braces; otherwise parameters may be lost or mis-parsed (20.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use \strut to keep interbaseline distances when reusing boxed paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Include vertical struts in boxed paragraphs you plan to copy so that interline distances remain correct when boxes are appended to vertical lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two struts are used if the message might be more than one line so there will be a strut at both top and bottom; if known to be a single line, struts may be omitted (20.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders: choose \leaders, \cleaders, or \xleaders appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: \leaders, \cleaders, and \xleaders distribute repeated boxes differently across the glue; choose the kind that matches alignment needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: \leaders: two boxes starting at 100pt, 110pt; \cleaders: three boxes starting at 95pt, 105pt, 115pt; \xleaders: three boxes staggered (21.4). You can define custom leader fills (21.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep leaders from disappearing at page or line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent leaders from disappearing at the top of a page or at a break use constructs like \null\nobreak and choose appropriate glue (filll) to overtake \parfillskip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: \null\nobreak\leaders\hrule\hskip10pt plus1filll\par keeps leaders and prevents them from vanishing at a line break or page top (21.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interline glue and vboxes: use \nointerlineskip when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Interline glue is added for vboxes but not for rules; when combining vboxes and rules you may need \nointerlineskip before and after constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you create a box and then move it with \moveright or place rules, remember to insert \nointerlineskip to avoid unexpected extra interline glue (21.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Default rule height/depth behavior without explicit specs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a \vrule has no explicit height or depth, it extends to the smallest enclosing box and may produce an overly heavy band.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid huge black bands, always give explicit height and depth for rules unless you intend the rule to fill the enclosing box; \leaders\vrule\vfill works fine in vertical mode (21.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral and multiple-integral spacing tweaks
rubrics_metrics.description: When typesetting multiple integral signs, small kerns like \! or \!\! can improve spacing between consecutive integral signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using three \!s between consecutive integral signs in a display may look best; but text style may prefer only two (18.33).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix and diagram baseline control
rubrics_metrics.description: When building commutative diagrams or matrices, reset and define \normalbaselines (baseline skip, lineskip, lineskiplimit) so the baseline behavior is consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided show defining \normalbaselines and macros \mapright and \mapdown for diagrams; ensure baselines are returned to expected values since other commands (like \openup) may have changed them (18.46).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious changing character codes and category codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering category codes or end-of-line handling (e.g., changing \endlinechar or setting a character to comment) can have subtle side effects; test thoroughly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include redefining \endlinechar to -1 to avoid inserted endline characters, or special tricks to strip trailing spaces; these may fail if names contain control sequences or unusual characters (20.18–20.19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Macros and expansion tricks: use \expandafter, \toks, and \edef carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructing macros that depend on expanded content requires careful use of \expandafter, \toks registers and \edef to get the desired expansion order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example techniques: use \toks0={\c} and \toks2=\expandafter{\d} before an \edef to assemble a macro with some parts expanded and others not (20.15). These are advanced but essential for robust macro programming.
